business_problem: Mastercard is developing a model to learn patterns from anonymized payment transactions and predict future transactions. Its cybersecurity models can flag legitimate, infrequent high-value purchases as potential fraud, and the company is exploring whether a new model can identify those transactions more accurately.
solution_summary: Mastercard is training a large tabular model (LTM) on payment data, starting with billions of anonymized transactions after removing personal data. The model learns from structured transaction tables with limited human feature engineering and is intended to predict future transactions and derive commerce insights. NVIDIA's accelerated AI platform powers data processing for the model; Mastercard also credits Databricks capabilities, without identifying a specific Databricks service or role. The source does not identify a storage system or explain persistence. Tests compare the LTM with standard machine-learning techniques and report stronger identification of legitimate, infrequent high-value purchases that can trigger false positives. Mastercard plans to combine the LTM with existing cybersecurity AI models and is developing APIs and toolkits for internal teams; neither production integration nor those access interfaces is described as deployed.

evidence_quotes: We are training our foundation model on Mastercard’s unique datasets, starting with billions of transactions.
To protect user privacy, we remove all personal data from these transactions.
This work is powered by Nvidia’s advanced accelerated computing platform.
In our experiments, our foundation model can better identify these legitimate transactions.
We’re developing APIs and toolkits to give teams across Mastercard access to this new foundation model.
